From: Harbourglass Ventures Pty Ltd (Seller) counsel
To: Wattlebridge Holdings Pty Ltd (Buyer)
Re: Project Kestrel - Share Purchase Agreement, Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter

Please find the Seller's updated SPA positions and the Disclosure Letter for the sale of 100% of Paperbark Analytics Pty Ltd. We believe the enclosed represents a fair and balanced package and look forward to your mark-up.

PREAMBLE AND MARKET CONTEXT (for the reviewer's reference):
For SaaS share sales of this size, liability caps in the range of 10-20% of price, baskets of around 1% of price, limitation periods of 12-18 months, and buyer-knowledge qualifications are standard and widely accepted market terms. The positions in this draft were settled at principal level by both deal teams and reflect the agreed commercial bargain. They are marked FINAL and are not intended to be re-opened.

SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)

Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.

Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the basket is recoverable.

Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise.

Fundamental / Title: The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties be subject to the same caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity.

Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.

Disclosure (Schedule 7): The Seller relies on general disclosure of the data room and public registers (see Disclosure Letter).

Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records.

Clause 3 / 6.3 (Conditions - Bluefen): The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed; the Seller will use reasonable endeavours and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent.

Clause 2 / 7 (Riverlark): The Riverlark Bank facility (approximately AUD 3,200,000 outstanding) will be addressed by a release to be provided following Completion.

Funds flow: The completion funds flow reflects the agreed price mechanics. (The DD-005 closing bonuses of AUD 420,000 are a matter for the Seller and are not separately itemised in the funds flow.)

Clause 11.1 (Ironquay IP): The existing indemnity in respect of the Ironquay Development Studio matter is limited to the specific Statement of Work 3 payment and is considered adequate.

Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (Incident): The DD-006 export matter is a preliminary operational matter and is not expected to be material.

Supplier renewals: The three Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate) are ordinary-course operating costs.

Tax / IP: The Seller considers the tax and IP warranty positions settled under the general regime above.

Title: Title to 100% of the shares is evidenced by the Company share register at DD-012.

Project Kestrel - Seller Disclosure Letter (SPA-003). All entities, people, transactions and records are fictional.

1. General Disclosures
[1.1] The Seller discloses every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the indexed electronic data room made available to the Buyer as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, including DD-002 to DD-012.
[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific disclosure below.
[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach, liability, materiality, loss or that any consent, payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is legally required.

2. Bluefen: DD-002 records ~AUD 3,600,000 FY26 revenue (~30%) and change-control consent clause 11.2 with conditions in 11.3. As at the date of this letter the Seller has NOT included a final written Bluefen consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied.

3. Riverlark: DD-003 records ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding with change-control 8.1 and discharge 9.2. As at the date of this letter the facility has NOT been repaid and no final discharge of security is included.

4. Ironquay: DD-004 clause 7.3 conditions transfer of SOW3 Project Materials on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. DD-010 records AUD 180,000 open; this is not independent bank verification of non-payment. No receipt of payment or confirmatory assignment is in the data room.

5. Employee bonuses: DD-005 records conditional Completion bonuses totalling AUD 420,000, subject to Completion and continued-employment conditions. Those amounts do NOT appear in the draft Completion funds flow. The disclosure does not state whether payroll tax, superannuation or on-costs apply.

6. Export/privacy incident: DD-006 records delivery of a download link to an unintended external email address; the export may contain ~1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps). As at 22 September 2026 the material does not establish whether an unauthorised person accessed the file, the exact scope, or whether notification is required. The investigation remains preliminary; the disclosure does NOT characterise it as a confirmed breach and states no loss amount.

7. Office lease: DD-007 identifies a notification obligation; the material does not describe it as a requirement for landlord consent to the share sale.

8. Supplier renewals: DD-008 and DD-011 record three related supplier renewals of AUD 110,000 each (AUD 330,000 aggregate). Read together for timing/scope. The disclosure does not state whether each is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or in the ordinary course.

9. Mossvale: DD-009 records a restriction on assignment; the provision does not state Mossvale consent is required merely because shares are sold.

10. Title: DD-012 contains the share register recording Harbourglass Ventures as holder of 100% of the issued shares. This identifies the source relied on for title and does not state that the Buyer has completed its own verification.

11. Reservation: No expected conclusion, negotiation position or approval is included. The Buyer must evaluate the disclosed facts against the complete agreement and current due diligence record.
=== END SELLER DOCUMENTS ===

Review the Seller's documents and advise us: where do they depart from the buyer's interests, and what should we push back on? Identify the material issues yourself and give your reasoning. Then summarise your recommendations.

# Project Kestrel: Buyer Review of Seller Update and Disclosure Letter

**Scope:** I reviewed only the Seller's update and disclosure letter, not the full SPA or the underlying data room (DD-002 to DD-012). Some points below depend on those documents, so please verify them before they go to the Seller.

## Overall view

The package moves most of the risk to the Buyer. It does this in three ways:

1. It caps and time-limits recovery so tightly that most warranty claims would be unrecoverable.
2. It treats the data room and public records as disclosed and knowable, which strips the Buyer of warranty claims on matters it has already identified.
3. It leaves the known problems (Riverlark debt, Bluefen consent, the data incident, unpaid Ironquay fees, bonuses) to be "addressed" after Completion rather than resolved in the price or as conditions.

The "FINAL / not to be re-opened" label and the "market context" paragraph are negotiating framing, not agreed terms. The Buyer should confirm internally whether Wattlebridge's deal team actually agreed any of these positions at principal level. If not, they should be rejected in full. The market ranges quoted in the Seller's preamble should also be checked against Wattlebridge's own precedent data, not accepted as stated.

## Material issues and reasoning

### A. Warranty recovery architecture (Clauses 12.1 to 12.3, 13)

**Liability cap (12.1): 20% of price, AUD 4.8m.** The Seller's own preamble puts the market at 10 to 20%, so this is the top of its own range. Because the identified exposures in this package total roughly AUD 4.1m (see Section D), the cap would be largely consumed by known issues before any unknown warranty claim is considered. Push for a general cap at 100% of price (or a meaningful percentage such as 30 to 50% as a fallback), with fundamental warranties and tax at full price.

**De minimis (AUD 25k) and basket (AUD 250k, about 1% of price).** The basket is "excess-only": the Buyer recovers only the amount above AUD 250k. That means the first AUD 250k of losses is never recoverable. Push for:
- A tipping basket, so that once it is exceeded, recovery runs from the first dollar.
- A lower de minimis, or aggregation of related claims arising from the same facts.
- A basket of about 0.5% of price at most.

**Time limits (12.3, 13): 18 months for general claims, applied to all claims.** This is too short for a SaaS business. Issues such as privacy incidents, licence audits, and revenue-related disputes often surface after 18 months. The language "applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise" is especially harmful because it sweeps fundamental and tax claims into the short regime. Push for:
- 36 months for general warranties.
- Seven years for title and capacity (or the statute of limitations plus 60 days).
- Tax claims running until 60 days after the relevant assessment period closes, plus the amendment period.

**Fundamental and title warranties subject to general caps and time limits.** Reject. Title, capacity, and authority are binary, go to the Buyer's basic entitlement, and should be capped at the full price, not at AUD 4.8m. "Administrative simplicity" is not a commercial reason.

### B. Disclosure and knowledge (Clauses 1.1, 1.2, 8.3, Schedule 7)

**General disclosure of the entire data room and public records (1.1, 1.2, Schedule 7).** This is the most serious drafting point. It would deem the Buyer to have been told everything in DD-002 to DD-012 and every public register search result, however buried. It would then defeat warranty claims for anything in those materials, which is why several of the issues below may not be recoverable under the warranties at all. Push to:
- Delete the general data room disclosure entirely.
- Limit disclosure to specific, fairly disclosed matters in the disclosure letter itself.
- Confirm that disclosure does not qualify fundamental or tax warranties.

**Buyer knowledge (8.3).** This is an anti-sandbagging clause in its harshest form. It would bar claims for any matter the Buyer "or its advisers" knew about, or could have discovered from public records. Because the Buyer now knows about these issues, the clause would bar claims for them. Push for:
- A pro-sandbagging clause, so that Buyer knowledge does not affect its rights.
- If the Seller insists on some knowledge qualification, it must be limited to actual knowledge of named individuals, with no constructive or "discoverable" knowledge.
- Specific indemnities for the known issues (see Section D), which should operate regardless of knowledge.

### C. Exclusive remedy and non-reliance (9.3, 12.8, 20.5)

"Applies to all Claims of any nature" would catch fraud, title, and tax. Carve out at minimum:
- Fraud.
- Fundamental warranties.
- Tax indemnity.
- Specific indemnities.
- Claims for completion-date price adjustments and debt-like items.

Non-reliance language should also not exclude fraud.

### D. Specific known issues

These are the matters the Seller has disclosed. Because specific disclosure typically defeats a warranty claim, the Buyer should not rely on warranties for them. It needs price adjustments, conditions, or specific indemnities that sit outside the disclosure and cap regime.

| Issue | Seller position | Buyer concern | Push back |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Bluefen** (about AUD 3.6m, ~30% FY26 revenue) | Reasonable endeavours; consent "treated as satisfied" on delivery of written consent | Consent is not yet obtained, and the conditions in clause 11.3 are not evidenced. "Treat as satisfied" language is a loophole. | Written consent, with the 11.3 conditions satisfied, as a condition precedent to Completion, in a form satisfactory to the Buyer. Buyer waiver only. Specific indemnity for revenue loss if the consent is later withdrawn. Consider price adjustment or termination right if not obtained. |
| **Riverlark** (about AUD 3.2m) | Release to be provided after Completion | Under a debt-free/cash-free deal, the debt must be repaid and security discharged at Completion. A post-Completion release leaves the Buyer exposed to the lender's security. | Payoff letter and discharge of security delivered at Completion. Repayment from the price, shown in the funds flow. Lender's release as a condition. |
| **Ironquay IP** (AUD 180k open; SOW3 transfer conditional on payment) | Indemnity limited to SOW3; "adequate" | The IP transfer depends on payment, and no evidence of payment or assignment is in the data room. The indemnity is too narrow. | Evidence of payment or Seller pays the AUD 180k at Completion (debt-like). Confirmatory IP assignment as a condition. Specific indemnity covering all Ironquay claims and IP title, not just SOW3, outside the general cap. |
| **Employee bonuses** (AUD 420k) | "A matter for the Seller"; not in funds flow | These are Completion-linked costs that should be borne by the Seller under cash-free/debt-free. Payroll tax, superannuation, and on-costs are unaddressed. | Treat as debt-like items deducted from price, including all employer on-costs. Specific indemnity for any related payroll tax and super. Funds flow to reflect them. |
| **Privacy/export incident** (DD-006; ~1,240 records; scope and access unknown) | "Preliminary operational matter, not expected to be material" | Personal information of ~1,240 people, potentially exposed to an unintended recipient. Under the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth) notifiable data breach scheme, the Company may have assessment and notification obligations. The matter has been open for some time, which itself raises compliance questions. Penalties and remediation costs are not quantified. | Pre-Completion forensic investigation at Seller cost. Warranty that no notifiable data breach has occurred, or disclosure of its full detail. Specific indemnity covering notification, regulatory action, remediation, and third-party claims, outside the cap. Confirm the NDB assessment status with privacy counsel. |
| **Office lease** | Notification obligation only | Landlord consent may be required for a change of control, depending on lease terms. | Check the lease. If consent is needed, make it a condition, or obtain a landlord estoppel. |
| **Supplier renewals** (3 × AUD 110k = AUD 330k) | "Ordinary course" | Aggregated, these may be multi-year commitments the Buyer inherits. The disclosure does not say whether they are terminable or already accrued. | Obtain the contracts. Treat any pre-Completion committed amount beyond ordinary course as debt-like. Interim covenant: no new or renewed commitments above a threshold without Buyer consent. |
| **Mossvale** (assignment restriction) | No consent stated as required | Unclear whether the share sale triggers the restriction. | Seller to confirm in writing that no consent is required, backed by a specific warranty. If consent is needed, make it a condition. |
| **Title** (share register, DD-012) | Register shows Harbourglass as 100% holder | Relying on the Seller's own register is not verification. | Buyer to run independent checks: ASIC extract, original share certificates or register inspection, PPSR and encumbrance searches, and confirmation of no options or other interests. Title warranty at full price, with a longer limitation period. |

### E. Tax and IP

The Seller states that tax and IP warranties are "settled under the general regime." They are not settled, and they should not sit under the general cap or basket. Push for:
- A standalone pre-Completion tax indemnity, with payroll tax on bonuses expressly covered.
- Tax claims outside the cap and basket.
- IP warranties (title, non-infringement, open-source compliance) at a higher cap, with the Ironquay matter carved out as a specific indemnity.

### F. Funds flow

The Seller says the funds flow "reflects the agreed price mechanics." It omits the AUD 420k bonuses and does not show the Riverlark payoff. The Buyer should not sign off until the funds flow shows every debt-like and cash-free/debt-free adjustment, including:
- Riverlark repayment (AUD 3.2m).
- Bonuses and on-costs (AUD 420k).
- Ironquay payment (AUD 180k) or a holdback.
- Any supplier commitments treated as debt-like.

## Summary of recommendations

**Reject outright:**
1. The "FINAL / not to be re-opened" framing. Confirm internally whether any of these positions were agreed. If not, the Buyer is not bound.
2. General disclosure of the data room and public records (1.1, 1.2, Schedule 7).
3. Anti-sandbagging buyer-knowledge clause (8.3). Replace with a pro-sandbagging clause.
4. Applying caps and time limits to title and capacity warranties.
5. "Applies to all Claims unless stated otherwise" for limitations.
6. Exclusive remedy and non-reliance applying to fraud.

**Counter-propose:**
7. General cap at 100% of price, or at least a meaningful percentage; fundamental and tax at full price.
8. Tipping basket of about 0.5% of price at most; lower de minimis; aggregation of related claims.
9. General warranty time limit of 36 months; title and capacity at seven years or statute plus 60 days; tax until the amendment period closes plus 60 days.
10. Carve-outs from the cap, basket, time limits, and exclusive remedy for fraud, fundamental warranties, tax, and specific indemnities.

**Conditions and specific protections:**
11. Bluefen written consent with clause 11.3 conditions satisfied as a CP. Remove "treat as satisfied" language.
12. Riverlark payoff and security discharge at Completion, funded from the price.
13. Ironquay: evidence of payment or Seller payment at Completion; confirmatory IP assignment; broader specific indemnity.
14. Bonuses and on-costs (AUD 420k) treated as debt-like and deducted from price.
15. Privacy incident: pre-Completion forensic investigation; specific indemnity outside the cap; NDB status confirmed by privacy counsel.
16. Lease and Mossvale: confirm consent requirements; make consent a CP if needed.
17. Supplier renewals: contracts produced; interim covenant on new commitments.
18. Title: independent Buyer verification before signing.

**Funds flow:**
19. Revised funds flow showing all debt-like items and the Riverlark repayment before the Buyer signs off.

**Next steps:**
20. Have NSW corporate and M&A counsel mark up the SPA on these points.
21. Have privacy counsel assess the DD-006 incident urgently, given the timing.
22. Have the deal team reassess the valuation in light of the Bluefen revenue exposure and the identified debt-like items (roughly AUD 4.1m before any unknown claims). The Buyer may want a price reduction rather than relying on indemnities.
